title: Overview and justification
body:
This course is about building a revision strategy: turning the time before an exam into a plan that actually works. By the end you will be able to build a strategy around your use of time and the gaps in your knowledge, apply active-learning principles rather than relying on passive review, and select revision techniques that fit the material you are studying.

You already know that exams need a strategy. This course is where you build one. A good strategy is not about revising for longer; it is about revising in the right way, on the right things, at the right time.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: build a revision strategy around your use of time and the gaps in your knowledge
apply active-learning principles to revision, distinguishing active techniques from passive review
select active revision techniques across visual, auditory and kinaesthetic approaches to fit your material.

title: In real academic practice
body: A revision strategy is not just something you need for exams. The same habits, planning your time against your goals, finding the gaps in what you know, and working actively rather than passively, are how you manage any large piece of work. Build the strategy now and you build a way of working that carries through your degree and into professional life.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, the anatomy of a revision strategy: the two things it is built on. Second, active revision rather than passive review: why how you revise matters more than how long. Third, choosing active techniques: the visual, auditory and kinaesthetic toolkit you select from. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: Orientation
body: You already know a revision strategy matters. This lesson is about what one is actually made of. A strategy is not a timetable that blocks out every hour, nor a promise to work harder. It is a plan built on two simple things: how you use your time, and how well you know where your knowledge is thin. Get those two right and the rest follows.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are moving from knowing that you need a strategy to building one. You are not yet expected to run a fully self-directed revision programme across a whole year. The aim is to assemble a workable strategy for a module, and to understand why it is built the way it is.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: identify the two elements an effective revision strategy is built on: your use of time and your ability to spot gaps in your knowledge
recognise, in a worked example, how a student turns a vague plan into a strategy built on time and gaps
plan the stages of a revision strategy for a module in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
An effective revision strategy is built on two elements: your use of time, and your ability to identify gaps in your knowledge and understanding. Time is finite, so a strategy decides where it goes. Gaps are what revision is for, so a strategy has to find them before it can close them. A plan that ignores either one is just a wish.

Managing those two under pressure takes what the book calls cognitive resilience: the ability to stay focused on your objectives while the stress of revision and exams pulls at your attention. A strategy supports resilience by giving you clear objectives and visible progress, so you always know what to do next.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about how you revised for your last set of exams. Did you plan your time around where your knowledge was thinnest, or did you spread it evenly and hope? What is one thing you would change?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: A revision strategy is built on two elements: your use of time and your ability to identify gaps in your knowledge. The stages of a strategy map the ground, find the gaps, budget the time against them, revise actively, then review and adjust. Holding to those objectives under pressure is cognitive resilience. You can now recognise a real strategy and plan one of your own. The next lesson is about revising actively rather than passively.

title: Orientation
body: In the last lesson you built the frame of a strategy. This lesson is about what you put inside it. Two students can spend the same number of hours revising and come out knowing very different amounts. The difference is not time; it is whether the revision was active or passive. This lesson shows what that difference looks like and why it matters.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are learning to choose how you revise, not just how long. You are not yet expected to design elaborate active-learning sequences. The aim is to tell active revision from passive, understand why active works better, and swap a passive habit for an active one.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: distinguish active revision from passive review
recognise, in a worked example, the active move a student makes instead of re-reading passively
choose an active technique to replace a passive revision habit in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Passive revision takes knowledge in without asking you to do anything with it. Re-reading notes, highlighting a chapter, or copying a definition all feel like work, but they let the material wash over you. You recognise it on the page and mistake that for knowing it. Under exam conditions, recognition is not enough.

Active revision makes you recreate or apply the knowledge. You close the book and try to recall it, you test yourself, you explain an idea in your own words, or you solve a problem with it. This is harder, which is exactly why it works: the effort of retrieving and using knowledge is what fixes it in memory and builds your confidence that you can produce it when it counts.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a revision habit you rely on. Is it active or passive? If it is passive, what active technique could you use instead to do the same job better?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Active revision beats passive review because it makes you recreate or apply knowledge rather than simply take it in. Re-reading and highlighting build recognition; recalling, testing and explaining build the retrieval you need in an exam. You can now tell the two apart and swap a passive habit for an active one. The next lesson gives you a toolkit of active techniques to choose from.

title: Orientation
body: You know now that revision should be active. This lesson gives you the toolkit. Active techniques fall into three families: visual, auditory and kinaesthetic. Each works with knowledge in a different way, and each suits some material better than others. Knowing the families lets you pick the right tool for what you are revising, rather than using the same one for everything.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are learning to select techniques, not just to name them. You are not yet expected to invent your own methods or run them under exam pressure. The aim is to know the three families, match a technique to its family, and choose techniques that fit the material in front of you.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: describe the visual, auditory and kinaesthetic families and match a technique to its family
recognise, in a worked example, how a student selects techniques to fit the material
select active techniques that fit the material you revise in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Active techniques group into three families. Visual techniques use imagery, colour, pattern and spatial layout: mind maps, visual notes, flashcards, diagrams and posters. Auditory techniques use listening and speaking: reading aloud, recording and replaying notes, and talking ideas through in a group. Kinaesthetic techniques use movement and touch: laying cards out in space, acting a process out, or moving while you recite.

No family is better than the others. The skill is matching the technique to the material. A structure with many linked parts suits a mind map; a set of terms suits flashcards or reading aloud; a procedure you perform suits a kinaesthetic walk-through. Choosing well is what makes the technique active for you.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Pick a topic you will need to revise soon. Which family of techniques fits its material best, and which single technique would you try first?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Active techniques fall into three families: visual, which uses imagery and layout; auditory, which uses listening and speaking; and kinaesthetic, which uses movement and touch. None is better than the others; the skill is matching the technique to the material. You can now describe the families, place a technique in its family, and choose techniques that fit what you are revising. With a strategy, active habits and a toolkit, you are ready to revise on purpose.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. A revision strategy is no longer a vague intention: it is something you can build and fill. You can name the two elements it rests on, your use of time and the gaps in your knowledge, and plan its stages. You can tell active revision from passive review and say why active works better. And you can choose techniques from the visual, auditory and kinaesthetic families to fit your material. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

Each time you plan your time against your gaps, choose an active technique over a passive one, and match the method to the material, you are using what this course gave you. The same planning and active habits serve any large task you take on, in study and in work.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The stages of a revision strategy
body: A revision strategy runs through five stages, from mapping the ground to adjusting the plan. Move through each stage to see what it asks of you.
instruction: Select each stage to reveal what it involves. Work through all five.

_items.title: Map the ground
_items.body: List every topic the exam could cover, taken from the module objectives. You cannot plan for what you have not written down.

_items.title: Find the gaps
_items.body: Test yourself on each topic to see what you can and cannot yet recall. This turns a vague worry into a clear list of weak spots.

_items.title: Budget the time
_items.body: Work back from the exam date and give more time to the gaps than to what you already know well. Time is finite, so spend it where it counts.

_items.title: Revise actively
_items.body: Fill each slot with an active technique that makes you recall or use the knowledge, rather than simply re-reading it.

_items.title: Review and adjust
_items.body: Re-test, see what has moved, and redirect the time that is left. Staying focused and adjusting under pressure is cognitive resilience at work.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: From passive to active
body: Four common revision habits, and the active move that does the same job better. Read each card to see the shift.
instruction: Read through the cards below.
ariaRegion: Passive habits and their active alternatives.

_items.title: Read it again, or recall it?
_items.subtitle: From passive to active
_items.text: Re-reading a page lets it feel familiar. Closing the book and trying to recall it shows what you actually know, and the effort of retrieving it is what makes it stick.

_items.title: Highlight, or rebuild?
_items.subtitle: From passive to active
_items.text: Highlighting marks a line as important but does nothing with it. Rebuilding the idea as a diagram or in your own words forces you to understand how it fits together.

_items.title: Copy notes, or test yourself?
_items.subtitle: From passive to active
_items.text: Copying notes keeps your hand busy and your mind idle. Turning them into questions and testing yourself makes you produce the answer, which is what the exam will ask.

_items.title: Recognise, or retrieve?
_items.subtitle: The key difference
_items.text: Passive revision builds recognition: you know it when you see it. Active revision builds retrieval: you can produce it from memory. Only retrieval helps in the exam room.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Three families of active technique
body: Active techniques group into three families. Open each to see what it draws on and the techniques it holds.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all three.

_items.title: Visual
_items.body: Visual techniques use imagery, colour, pattern and spatial layout to represent knowledge. They suit material with structure and connections. Techniques include mind mapping, visual note-taking, flashcards, visual mnemonics, and posters or infographics you can display and revisit.

_items.title: Auditory
_items.body: Auditory techniques draw on listening and speaking. They suit material you can rehearse in words. Techniques include reading your notes aloud, recording and replaying them, and talking ideas through in a discussion group, where explaining to others tests your own understanding.

_items.title: Kinaesthetic
_items.body: Kinaesthetic techniques use physical movement and touch to anchor memory. They suit processes and sequences. Techniques include laying cards out in space, role-playing a procedure, moving while you recite, and building or handling models of what you are learning.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students have a month before the same exam, and the same notes.

{{learner-a}} writes a timetable that gives every topic an equal block of time and plans to re-read the notes for each one. It looks organised. But {{learner-a}} has not asked where the knowledge is weak, so the strong topics get as much time as the shaky ones, and nothing tests whether the re-reading is working. This is a timetable, not a strategy.

{{learner-b}} starts differently. {{learner-b}} lists every topic the exam could cover, then does a quick test on each to see which ones are shaky. The weak topics get the most time, the secure ones get a short check, and each slot uses an active technique rather than re-reading. A week in, {{learner-b}} re-tests and shifts the plan to where the gaps remain. This is a strategy.

Both students planned their month. Only {{learner-b}} built the plan around time and gaps, which is what makes it a revision strategy.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students sit down to revise the same topic for two hours.

{{learner-a}} reads through the notes, highlights the important lines, and reads them again. By the end the pages look well used and the material feels familiar. But {{learner-a}} has only recognised the content, not produced it. Asked a question on it the next day, {{learner-a}} can picture the page but cannot quite recall the answer. This is passive review.

{{learner-b}} reads the notes once, then closes them. {{learner-b}} writes out the topic from memory, checks what was missed, turns the gaps into questions, and answers them again later without looking. It feels harder and slower. But the next day {{learner-b}} can recall the topic, because the effort of retrieving it is what fixed it. This is active revision.

Both students spent two hours. Only {{learner-b}} made the knowledge retrievable, by recreating it rather than re-reading it.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students revise the same module, which has three very different topics: a branching process, a set of key terms, and a theory with many linked parts.

{{learner-a}} likes flashcards, so {{learner-a}} makes flashcards for all three topics. The terms suit cards well. But the branching process becomes a muddle of cards in no order, and the linked theory loses the connections that matter most. The technique was fine; using the same one for everything was not. This is choosing a method before looking at the material.

{{learner-b}} looks at each topic first. The key terms become flashcards. The branching process is acted out as a physical walk-through, a kinaesthetic method that keeps the order clear. The linked theory becomes a mind map that lays the parts out and shows how they connect. Each technique was chosen to fit what the topic is. This is selecting techniques to fit the material.

Both students revised all three topics. Only {{learner-b}} matched the technique to the material rather than forcing one method onto everything.

title: Building the strategy
displayTitle: How to do it
body: These steps turn the two elements into a working strategy. Use them to build one for your next exam.
instruction: Tick each item once you have done it.

_items.text: Have I listed every topic the exam could cover, from the module objectives?
Have I tested myself to find where my knowledge is actually weak?
Have I given the weak topics more time than the secure ones?
Have I planned an active technique for each slot, not just re-reading?
Have I built in a point to re-test and adjust the plan?
Do I know what my next objective is whenever I sit down to revise?

title: Making revision active
displayTitle: How to do it
body: These moves turn a passive session into an active one. Try them on your next topic.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I closed the notes and tried to recall the topic from memory?
Have I turned my notes into questions and tested myself?
Have I explained the idea in my own words, aloud or in writing?
Have I applied the knowledge to a problem or example?
Have I checked what I missed, rather than assuming I knew it?
Have I noticed when a method only builds recognition, not retrieval?

title: Choosing a technique
displayTitle: How to do it
body: Use these questions to match a technique to the material in front of you.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I looked at what the material is before choosing a method?
Is this a structure with linked parts that a visual map would show?
Is this a set of terms that flashcards or reading aloud would drill?
Is this a process or sequence that a kinaesthetic walk-through would fix?
Have I picked the technique to fit the topic, not just my habit?
Have I checked that the technique makes me recall or use the knowledge?

title: Formative check: the two elements
displayTitle: An effective revision strategy is built on two elements. Which pair?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which pair are the two elements of a revision strategy?

_items.text: Your use of time, and your ability to spot gaps in your knowledge.
_items.feedback: Yes. Time and gaps are the two elements a strategy is built on.

_items.text: The number of hours you revise, and how early you begin.
_items.feedback: Hours and an early start help, but the strategy is about how you use time, not just how much.

_items.text: How neat your notes are, and how many of them you make.
_items.feedback: Tidy, plentiful notes are not a strategy; what matters is time and gaps.

_items.text: Your natural memory, and how much you enjoy the subject.
_items.feedback: A strategy works with your use of time and your gaps, whatever your memory or interest.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A revision strategy is built on your use of time and your ability to identify gaps in your knowledge.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the pair that is about where your time goes and where your knowledge is thin.
_incorrect.final: A revision strategy is built on your use of time and your ability to identify gaps in your knowledge. Hours, neat notes and natural memory are not the two elements.

title: Formative check: recognising a strategy
displayTitle: In the worked example, what turned the second student's plan into a real revision strategy?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What turned the second student's plan into a strategy?

_items.text: They worked out where their knowledge was weak and gave those topics the most time.
_items.feedback: Yes. Building the plan around gaps and time is what makes it a strategy.

_items.text: They planned to re-read every topic for an equal block of time.
_items.feedback: Equal blocks and re-reading describe the first student's timetable, not a strategy.

_items.text: They started revising earlier than the first student.
_items.feedback: Starting earlier is not the point; building around time and gaps is.

_items.text: They made a neater, more colourful timetable.
_items.feedback: How the plan looks does not make it a strategy; what it is built on does.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student built the plan around their gaps and spent time where it was needed, which is a strategy.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student built the plan around, rather than how it looked or when it started.
_incorrect.final: The plan became a strategy because it was built around where knowledge was weak and where time should go. A neat, equal, early timetable is not.

title: Formative check: planning a strategy
displayTitle: You are planning revision for a module in {{context}}. Which first step fits the strategy this lesson describes?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which first step fits the revision strategy this lesson describes?

_items.text: List the topics the exam could cover, then test yourself to find the gaps.
_items.feedback: Yes. Mapping the ground and finding the gaps is where a strategy in {{context}} begins.

_items.text: Start re-reading your notes from the first page onwards.
_items.feedback: Re-reading from the start is passive and ignores where your gaps are.

_items.text: Give every topic the same amount of time to be fair.
_items.feedback: Equal time ignores the gaps; the weak topics need more.

_items.text: Decide how many hours you can spare and fill them.
_items.feedback: Hours alone are not a plan; a strategy targets time at the gaps.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, a strategy begins by mapping the topics and testing yourself to find the gaps.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the step that finds where your knowledge is weak before spending time.
_incorrect.final: A strategy in {{context}} begins by listing the topics and testing yourself to find the gaps, then giving those gaps the time. Re-reading, equal time or counting hours do not.

title: Formative check: active versus passive
displayTitle: Which of these is active revision rather than passive review?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option is active revision rather than passive review?

_items.text: Closing your notes and trying to recall and explain a topic from memory.
_items.feedback: Yes. Recalling and explaining from memory is active revision.

_items.text: Reading your notes through again from start to finish.
_items.feedback: Re-reading builds recognition, not retrieval; it is passive.

_items.text: Highlighting the key lines in a chapter.
_items.feedback: Highlighting marks the text but does nothing with it; it is passive.

_items.text: Copying a definition out neatly into your notes.
_items.feedback: Copying keeps your hand busy but does not make you produce the knowledge.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Active revision makes you recreate or apply knowledge, such as recalling and explaining it from memory.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that makes you produce the knowledge, not just take it in again.
_incorrect.final: Active revision makes you recreate or apply knowledge, like recalling and explaining a topic. Re-reading, highlighting and copying only build recognition.

title: Formative check: the active move
displayTitle: In the worked example, what was the active move the second student made instead of re-reading?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What active move did the second student make instead of re-reading?

_items.text: They closed the notes and wrote the topic out from memory, then checked what they missed.
_items.feedback: Yes. Producing the topic from memory and checking it is the active move.

_items.text: They read the notes through more carefully than the first student.
_items.feedback: Reading more carefully is still passive; it does not produce the knowledge.

_items.text: They highlighted the most important lines first.
_items.feedback: Highlighting marks the text but does not make you retrieve it.

_items.text: They spent longer on the notes than the first student.
_items.feedback: More time on the same passive method is still passive review.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Writing the topic from memory and checking the gaps is active revision in action.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the move that made the student produce the knowledge, not re-read it.
_incorrect.final: The active move was to close the notes, write the topic from memory, and check what was missed. Reading more carefully, highlighting or spending longer are all still passive.

title: Formative check: replacing a passive habit
displayTitle: You usually revise a topic in {{context}} by re-reading your notes. Which active technique best replaces that habit?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which active technique best replaces re-reading your notes?

_items.text: Close the notes and write the topic out from memory, then check what you missed.
_items.feedback: Yes. Retrieving the topic from memory is the active replacement for re-reading in {{context}}.

_items.text: Read the notes more slowly and more times.
_items.feedback: Reading more slowly is still re-reading; the habit has not changed.

_items.text: Highlight the notes in a second colour.
_items.feedback: A second colour is still passive; nothing is being retrieved.

_items.text: Copy the notes out again by hand.
_items.feedback: Copying reproduces the notes without making you recall them.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Writing the topic from memory and checking it replaces re-reading with active retrieval in {{context}}.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that makes you produce the topic from memory, not read it again.
_incorrect.final: The active replacement is to write the topic from memory and check what you missed. Reading again, highlighting or copying all keep the habit passive.

title: Formative check: the families
displayTitle: Reading your notes aloud and recording them to replay belongs to which family of techniques?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Reading aloud and recording notes belongs to which family?

_items.text: Auditory.
_items.feedback: Yes. Listening and speaking are the auditory family.

_items.text: Visual.
_items.feedback: Visual techniques use imagery and layout, not listening and speaking.

_items.text: Kinaesthetic.
_items.feedback: Kinaesthetic techniques use movement and touch, not listening.

_items.text: None, because it is passive.
_items.feedback: Reading aloud and self-recording are active auditory techniques.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reading aloud and recording draw on listening and speaking, which is the auditory family.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which family is built on listening and speaking?
_incorrect.final: Reading aloud and recording notes are auditory techniques, built on listening and speaking. Visual uses imagery, and kinaesthetic uses movement.

title: Formative check: selecting to fit the material
displayTitle: In the worked example, why did the second student use a mind map for one topic and flashcards for another?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why did the second student use different techniques for different topics?

_items.text: They matched each technique to the kind of material, rather than using one method for everything.
_items.feedback: Yes. Matching the technique to the material is the skill this lesson teaches.

_items.text: They preferred variety and wanted their revision to feel less boring.
_items.feedback: The reason was fit, not variety for its own sake.

_items.text: They had run out of flashcards and had to improvise.
_items.feedback: The choice was deliberate, made to fit each topic.

_items.text: Mind maps are always better than flashcards.
_items.feedback: No technique is always better; the point is fit to the material.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student chose each technique to fit the kind of material, which is selecting to fit.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the reason that is about matching the method to the material.
_incorrect.final: The second student matched each technique to the kind of material, rather than forcing one method onto everything. It was not about variety, chance or one technique being best.

title: Formative check: choosing a technique
displayTitle: You are revising a topic in {{context}} that is a structure of many linked parts. Which technique fits it best?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which technique best fits a structure of many linked parts?

_items.text: A mind map that lays the parts out and shows how they connect.
_items.feedback: Yes. A visual map suits a structure of linked parts in {{context}}.

_items.text: Reading a single definition aloud over and over.
_items.feedback: Reading one definition aloud suits a term, not a linked structure.

_items.text: Copying the whole topic out word for word.
_items.feedback: Copying is passive and does not show how the parts connect.

_items.text: Highlighting the topic in your textbook.
_items.feedback: Highlighting marks the text but does not reveal the structure.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A mind map lays out a linked structure and shows the connections, which fits this material in {{context}}.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which technique shows how many parts connect to each other?
_incorrect.final: A structure of linked parts fits a visual mind map that shows the connections. Reading one definition aloud, copying or highlighting do not reveal the structure.

body: An effective revision strategy is built on two elements. Which pair?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which pair are the two elements of a revision strategy?

_items.text: Your use of time, and your ability to identify gaps in your knowledge.
_items.feedback: Yes. Time and gaps are the two elements.

_items.text: How many hours you revise, and how early you start.
_items.feedback: Hours and an early start are not the two elements.

_items.text: How neat and plentiful your notes are.
_items.feedback: Notes are not the two elements.

_items.text: Your natural memory and your interest in the subject.
_items.feedback: Memory and interest are not the two elements.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A strategy is built on your use of time and your ability to identify gaps.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about where your time goes and where your knowledge is thin.

body: What does cognitive resilience describe?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does cognitive resilience describe?

_items.text: Staying focused on your objectives while managing the pressure of revision and exams.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is cognitive resilience.

_items.text: Being able to revise for many hours without a break.
_items.feedback: Resilience is about focus under pressure, not endurance.

_items.text: Having a naturally strong memory for facts.
_items.feedback: It is not about natural memory.

_items.text: Feeling relaxed and never experiencing any stress.
_items.feedback: It is managing pressure, not avoiding it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Cognitive resilience is staying focused on your objectives while managing pressure.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. It is about holding your focus under pressure, not endurance or natural memory.

body: Which of these is active revision rather than passive review?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option is active revision rather than passive review?

_items.text: Closing your notes and recalling a topic from memory, then checking it.
_items.feedback: Yes. Recall and self-check is active.

_items.text: Reading your notes again from start to finish.
_items.feedback: Re-reading is passive.

_items.text: Highlighting the important lines.
_items.feedback: Highlighting is passive.

_items.text: Copying a definition out neatly.
_items.feedback: Copying is passive.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Recalling from memory and checking is active revision.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that makes you produce the knowledge.

body: Why does active revision work better than passive review?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why does active revision work better than passive review?

_items.text: Recreating or applying knowledge fixes it in memory better than taking it in again.
_items.feedback: Yes. The effort of retrieval is what fixes it.

_items.text: It always takes less time than passive review.
_items.feedback: Active revision is often harder and slower, not quicker.

_items.text: It feels easier and more comfortable.
_items.feedback: It usually feels harder, which is part of why it works.

_items.text: It avoids the need to understand the material.
_items.feedback: It deepens understanding rather than avoiding it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Recreating or applying knowledge fixes it better than simply taking it in again.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the effort of retrieving knowledge does.

body: Laying flashcards out in order and physically moving them as you recite belongs to which family?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Moving cards in space as you recite belongs to which family?

_items.text: Kinaesthetic.
_items.feedback: Yes. Movement and touch are kinaesthetic.

_items.text: Auditory.
_items.feedback: Auditory uses listening and speaking, not movement.

_items.text: Visual.
_items.feedback: The moving and handling makes it kinaesthetic, not simply visual.

_items.text: None, because it is passive.
_items.feedback: It is an active kinaesthetic technique.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Using movement and touch is the kinaesthetic family.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which family uses physical movement and touch?

body: A topic is a set of key terms and their definitions. Which technique fits it well?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which technique fits a set of key terms and definitions?

_items.text: Flashcards that test each term, or reading the definitions aloud.
_items.feedback: Yes. Terms suit flashcards or reading aloud.

_items.text: A single large diagram of the whole module.
_items.feedback: A whole-module diagram does not drill individual terms.

_items.text: Re-reading the glossary once.
_items.feedback: Re-reading is passive and does not test the terms.

_items.text: Acting out a physical procedure.
_items.feedback: A procedure suits a kinaesthetic method, not a list of terms.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A set of terms suits flashcards or reading the definitions aloud.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which technique drills individual terms and definitions?

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: the anatomy of a revision strategy, active revision rather than passive review, and choosing techniques that fit your material. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one revision practice you can keep using.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are not expected to run a flawless revision programme across a whole year. The aim is to see these three ideas as one connected practice rather than three separate parts, so it carries on past this course and through your degree.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: connect a revision strategy, active revision and techniques chosen to fit your material into one revision practice
analyse how the three strands work as one in a student's revision across a module
apply the three together to revise on purpose across your {{context}} study this term

title: Concept: definition
body: Revising on purpose is these three ideas working as one practice. You build a strategy around your time and your gaps, you fill it with active revision rather than passive review, and you choose techniques that fit each piece of material. The strategy decides where your effort goes, active revision makes that effort stick, and the right technique makes it fit the topic. Run together and adjusted as you go, they are one revision practice, not three separate parts.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, revising on purpose runs across a whole module, not just the week before the exam. You plan your time around your gaps, revise each topic actively, and pick a technique that fits it, then re-test and adjust. Each round feeds the next, so the practice improves as you go.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a module you will revise this term. How will you plan your time around your gaps, keep your revision active, and choose techniques that fit the material? When in your week will you run and review this practice?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Revising on purpose is most useful when the three ideas work as one practice. You plan around your time and gaps, revise actively, and choose techniques that fit the material, then repeat and adjust across the module. It is the practice, not any single session, that gets you ready for the exam.

title: The practice as one cycle
displayTitle: The practice as one cycle
body: The three ideas work as one continuing cycle, not three separate parts. Select each part of the cycle to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Map and test
_items.body: Map the topics and test yourself to find where your knowledge is weak, so you revise from evidence rather than a hunch.

_items.title: Budget time
_items.body: Budget more of your time to the weak topics than to the secure ones, so your effort goes where the gaps are.

_items.title: Revise actively
_items.body: Revise each topic actively rather than rereading it, choosing a technique that fits the material you are learning.

_items.title: Re-test
_items.body: Re-test to see what stuck, then carry what you learn into the next round and adjust the plan. The cycle keeps turning.

_diagram.title: Purposeful revision as a continuing cycle

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two students revise the same module. One makes a tidy timetable and re-reads every topic for an equal block of time. The other tests herself first, gives her weak topics the most time, revises them actively, and picks a technique to fit each one. By the exam, the second student knows her weak topics well, because she ran the three ideas as one practice.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: How to keep revising on purpose
body: Use these to keep the three ideas working together, rather than falling back into one habit for everything.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Have I planned my time around where my knowledge is weak, not spread it evenly?
Am I revising actively, rather than re-reading and highlighting?
Have I chosen each technique to fit the material, not just my habit?
Do I re-test and adjust the plan as I go, rather than setting it once?
Am I running this as one practice across the module, not a scramble before the exam?

displayTitle: Why is it better to treat strategy, active revision and technique choice as one practice rather than three separate ideas?
body: Why is it better to treat strategy, active revision and technique choice as one practice rather than three separate ideas?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it better to treat strategy, active revision and technique choice as one practice rather than three separate ideas?

_items.text: Because they depend on each other: the strategy decides where to work, active revision makes it stick, and the right technique fits the topic.
_items.feedback: Yes. Each part needs the others to do its job, so they work best run together.

_items.text: Because a timetable on its own is enough, as long as it looks organised.
_items.feedback: A timetable that ignores your gaps and uses passive review is not a working practice.

_items.text: Because the technique you pick matters more than your time or your gaps.
_items.feedback: No one part leads. The technique only helps once the strategy has pointed it at the right topic.

_items.text: Because doing all three means you never have to test yourself.
_items.feedback: Testing yourself is how you find your gaps. The practice depends on it, not avoids it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The three parts depend on each other, so they work best as one practice rather than three separate jobs.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how each part needs the other two to be any use.

displayTitle: A student lists her topics, tests herself to find the weak ones, gives them the most time, and revises each with a technique chosen to fit it. What does this show?
body: A student lists her topics, tests herself to find the weak ones, gives them the most time, and revises each with a technique chosen to fit it. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student lists her topics, tests herself to find the weak ones, gives them the most time, and revises each with a technique chosen to fit it. What does this show?

_items.text: One revision practice at work: a strategy built on time and gaps, filled with active revision and techniques that fit the material.
_items.feedback: Yes. All three ideas are running together as one practice.

_items.text: That she is spending too long on revision and should cut it down.
_items.feedback: The point is not how long she spends. It is that the three ideas work together.

_items.text: That the technique she picks is the only thing that matters.
_items.feedback: The technique only helps because the strategy pointed it at a weak topic first.

_items.text: That she has skipped planning and gone straight to revising.
_items.feedback: She planned first: she found her gaps and budgeted her time before revising.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Strategy, active revision and fitting techniques are all running together here, which is the whole practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at how many of the three ideas she is using at once.

displayTitle: You want to revise {{context}} on purpose this term. Which plan best brings the three ideas together into one practice?
body: You want to revise {{context}} on purpose this term. Which plan best brings the three ideas together into one practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to revise your subject on purpose this term. Which plan best brings the three ideas together into one practice?

_items.text: Find your weak topics, give them the most time, and revise each actively with a technique that fits the material.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs all three ideas together as one practice.

_items.text: Re-read every topic for an equal block of time until the exam.
_items.feedback: That spreads time evenly and stays passive, so none of the three ideas is really working.

_items.text: Pick your favourite technique and use it for every topic.
_items.feedback: One technique for everything ignores both your gaps and the shape of each topic.

_items.text: Leave it to the week before and revise whatever feels worst.
_items.feedback: Leaving it late skips the strategy. The three ideas need planning and repeating over the term.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Planning around your gaps, revising actively, and fitting the technique to the topic is the whole practice in action.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the plan that uses all three ideas, not just one.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: What does it mean to revise on purpose, as this course uses the phrase?
body: What does it mean to revise on purpose, as this course uses the phrase?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does it mean to revise on purpose, as this course uses the phrase?

_items.text: Running a strategy, active revision and well-chosen techniques together as one practice.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is the whole practice.

_items.text: Revising for as many hours as you possibly can.
_items.feedback: Purpose is about how you revise, not how long.

_items.text: Re-reading your notes until they feel familiar.
_items.feedback: That is passive review, not the full practice.

_items.text: Using one favourite technique for every topic.
_items.feedback: A technique only helps when it fits the topic and the plan.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A student plans her time around her weak topics, revises them actively, and chooses a mind map for a linked topic and flashcards for key terms. What is she doing?
body: A student plans her time around her weak topics, revises them actively, and chooses a mind map for a linked topic and flashcards for key terms. What is she doing?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student plans her time around her weak topics, revises them actively, and chooses a mind map for a linked topic and flashcards for key terms. What is she doing?

_items.text: Running all three ideas as one revision practice.
_items.feedback: Yes. Strategy, active revision and fitting techniques are all at work.

_items.text: Only choosing techniques, with no strategy behind it.
_items.feedback: She planned her time and gaps first, so there is a strategy.

_items.text: Only managing her time, with no active revision.
_items.feedback: She is revising actively, not just budgeting time.

_items.text: Revising passively by re-reading each topic.
_items.feedback: She is revising actively and choosing techniques, not re-reading.

_feedback.correct: Correct.
